Learning Objectives
Describe the bony and soft-tissue structures that confer stability to the glenohumeral joint.
Discuss the manner in which anterior glenoid bone loss contributes to recurrent glenohumeral
instability.
Explain the glenoid track concept.
Describe key history and physical examination findings in patients with recurrent
glenohumeral instability.
Explain how glenoid bone loss is measured.
Review patient and anatomic factors that should be considered in selecting appropriate
surgical management.

Pathophysiology and Pathoanatomy
Overview
Recurrent anterior glenohumeral instability may result from a spectrum of factors; one factor
is glenoid and/or humeral head bone loss.1
Left unmanaged, glenoid and/or humeral head bone loss may lead to recurrent glenohumeral
instability and poor patient satisfaction.
Glenohumeral bone loss compromises the equilibrium between shoulder mobility and stability
by altering the congruity of the joint.
Some studies estimate that 90% of shoulders with recurrent instability have glenoid rim
abnormalities.

Overview
The stability of the glenohumeral joint requires a complex interaction of soft-tissue and
bony structures. The glenoid is an important part of the concavity-compression
mechanism that provides glenohumeral stability. The anterior glenoid also serves as a
buttress against anterior instability. The glenoid labrum prevents instability; it is a
cartilaginous ring that deepens the glenoid fossa and serves as an attachment for the
capsuloligamentous structures. The glenohumeral ligaments form a second important
restraint; they attach to the glenoid and labrum. The anterior band of the inferior
glenohumeral ligament is the primary restraint to anterior translation of the humeral
head with the arm in abduction and external rotation. The posterior band of the inferior
glenohumeral ligament is the primary restraint to posterior translation of the humeral
head with the arm in forward flexion and adduction. The superior glenohumeral
ligament, middle glenohumeral ligament, and coracohumeral ligament also play
important roles in glenohumeral stability.

Epidemiology
The prevalence of glenoid bone loss in patients with recurrent instability is difficult to estimate;
however, as many as 90% to 100% of patients in whom instability repair fails have some
glenohumeral bone loss.1
The amount of bone loss is not reported consistently in the literature.
A lack of uniformity exists in evaluating the glenoid rim for bone defects.

Epidemiology
Variability exists in reporting the prevalence of glenoid bone loss and the manner in
which to measure it; however, some degree of glenoid deficiency can occur in as many
as 25% of patients after an initial dislocation. In addition, as many as 90% of patients
with recurrent instability or in whom prior stabilization failed have glenoid bone
deficiency.1 Dickens et al2 attempted to determine the amount of bone loss associated
with a single instability event in first-time dislocators. A total of 714 military athletes were
followed prospectively for 4 years. During that time, 23 first-time instability events and 6
recurrent instability events occurred. In patients with a first-time anterior instability
event, mean glenoid bone loss was 6.8%. In patients with recurrent instability, mean
glenoid bone loss was 22.8%. The authors concluded that glenoid bone loss can occur
after a single dislocation, and recurrent instability events result in additional bone loss.
Pathoanatomy
Initial glenohumeral dislocations may result in bony injury, which may lead to chronic
attritional changes.1
In patients with acute recurrent instability (less than 3 months), fracture fragments can be
reported.
Patients with chronic instability typically sustain erosive bone loss without identifiable fracture
fragments.

Loss of bone in the anteroinferior glenoid reduces the area available for articulation
between the glenoid and the humeral head, resulting in a smaller surface area to
prevent dislocation. In discussing glenoid bone loss, surgeons also must consider
humeral bone defects. Hill-Sachs lesions occur because of impaction of the
posterolateral humeral head against the anterior glenoid rim during an anterior
shoulder dislocation. Yamamoto et al3 developed the concept of a glenoid track to
account for the roles glenoid bone loss and humeral bone loss play in recurrent
instability. The glenoid track is defined as the zone of contact between the glenoid and
the humeral head. If the Hill-Sachs lesion is confined within the margins of the glenoid
contact area, the lesion is considered to be on track. If the Hill-Sachs lesion is larger than
or extends medial to the glenoid track, the risk of engagement increases, and the lesion
is considered to be off track. In addition, anterior glenoid bone loss alters the width of
the glenoid track and may convert an on-track Hill-Sachs defect into an unstable, off-
track lesion. Figure 1 shows the glenoid track concept4 (Resource 1).
Shaha et al5 attempted to determine whether the glenoid track concept was valid from a
clinical perspective. In their study, 57 shoulders were managed via arthroscopic Bankart
repair. Preoperative MRI was used to determine glenoid bone loss, the size of the Hill-
Sachs lesion, and whether the shoulders were on track or off track. Of the 49 patients
with an on-track shoulder,5 4 (8%) had recurrent instability, compared with 6 of the eight
patients (75%) with an off-track shoulder. This authors concluded that the glenoid track
concept is an accurate predictor of recurrent instability.5

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Surgeons must obtain a thorough patient history4
Determine the preinjury activity level and the events surrounding the initial dislocation
Assess the number of instability events before the first surgical procedure
Determine which activities lead to instability events
Prior management, both nonsurgical and surgical
Review prior surgical reports and imaging studies, if available
Degree of sport participation, recreational or competitive
Type of sport, such as contact or forced overhead
Pain and mechanical symptoms

Patient History
Patients with glenohumeral bone loss typically have an initial high-energy dislocation
followed by multiple low-energy or spontaneous instability episodes. In evaluating
patients with recurrent instability, surgeons must determine their activity level before
the initial injury. In addition, the events surrounding the initial dislocation provide
important details. Symptomatic instability associated with activities of daily living or
sleep should increase suspicion for attritional bone loss. Surgeons must review all prior
treatments, including a review of surgical reports and intraoperative images to
determine the appropriateness of prior surgical management. Lastly, surgeons must
discuss patient expectations to understand what type of activity the patient is seeking to
resume.6
Physical Examination
Inspection of the shoulder to identify deformity, scapular dyskinesia, the presence of surgical
scars, or rotator cuff atrophy1
Assess active and passive shoulder range of motion (ROM)
Rotator cuff strength, including subscapularis function

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies and the quantification of glenohumeral bone loss are important aspects of the
preoperative planning and decision-making processes.6
Radiography
Baseline imaging studies should include AP, scapular Y, and axillary views of the shoulder.
Anterior glenoid defects occasionally can be visualized on these images; however, advanced
imaging studies usually are required.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Can evaluate damage to labrum, cartilage, and capsule
Also can determine if a humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament lesion is present
(Figure 4; Resource 2).

Imaging Studies
Bishop et al7 attempted to identify the imaging modality most reliable in quantifying
glenoid bone loss. Anterior glenoid defects were created in cadaver model shoulders
and imaged via radiography, MRI, CT, and three dimensional CT. Twelve independent
blinded evaluators reviewed the images and estimated the percentage of glenoid bone
loss. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction images were associated with the highest
interobserver and intraobserver agreement among the evaluators. Three-dimensional
CT allows for reliable and reproducible estimation of glenoid bone loss and should be
included in the preoperative evaluation of patients with recurrent instability.
Various techniques to measure glenoid bone loss have been described in the literature.
No preferred technique exists; however, linear measurements are a popular choice in
clinical practice. The inferior glenoid resembles a circle; therefore, a best-fitting inferior
glenoid circle can be created. The width of the defect can be measured with a line and
then compared with the width of the inferior glenoid circle. The percentage of bone loss
can then be determined using the formula: percentage of bone loss = (width of
defect/width of inferior glenoid circle) × 100. The linear method is shown in Figure 6.4

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment has limited utility in patients with recurrent instability and glenoid bone
loss.1
Although some evidence exists for external rotation bracing in patients with a soft-tissue
Bankart lesion, the utility of this treatment option has not been studied in patients with bone
loss.
Physical therapy is the mainstay of nonsurgical management.

Focus on enhancing the dynamic stabilizing role of the periscapular and rotator cuff
musculature.
The goal is a stable arc during functional ROM.
As the degree of bone loss increases, nonsurgical management becomes increasingly
insufficient to maintain a stable shoulder.
Surgical Management
Surgical management is the mainstay of treatment for patients with recurrent instability and
bone loss.
Preoperative Planning and Decision-Making
Management of glenohumeral instability depends on patient risk factors and associated
pathology involving the glenoid and the humeral head.
Patient age, activity level, amount of glenoid bone loss, and the presence of an off-track Hill-
Sachs lesion are considered in determining the most appropriate surgical treatment option.
The critical amount of glenoid bone loss that necessitates bony augmentation continues to be
a subject of debate; however, glenoid bone loss greater than 20% is a commonly used cutoff.
Some studies advocate 13.5% as an appropriate threshold9 (Table 1)

Preoperative Planning and Decision-Making
Preoperative planning is essential in the treatment of patients with recurrent instability.
Patient age, sex, activity level, glenoid bone loss, and humeral head defects are
considered in determining the most appropriate surgical treatment option.
The critical amount of glenoid bone loss that necessitates bony augmentation continues
to be a subject of debate. More than 20% bone loss is a commonly used threshold to
consider bony augmentation of the glenoid defect; however, certain studies suggest a
lower threshold may be indicated. Dickens et al10 attempted to identify the effect of
subcritical bone loss (less than 20%) on recurrent instability in contact athletes. A total of
50 college football players were followed after arthroscopic stabilization surgery. Three

patients sustained recurrent instability, all of whom had bone loss greater than 13.5%.
No patients with bone loss less than 13.5% (47 patients) had recurrent instability events.
Bony augmentation procedures may be a treatment option for younger patients with
glenoid bone loss of 15% to 20% who seek to return to contact sports.11
The glenoid track concept also has been found to be predictive of recurrent instability.
The glenoid track is the contact area of the humeral head on the glenoid, which equals
84% of the total glenoid width. Shaha et al5 described the method used to determine
whether a shoulder is on track or off track: measure the diameter of the inferior glenoid
and glenoid bone loss (Figure 7). The glenoid track then is calculated as glenoid track =
(0.83 × diameter of the inferior glenoid) minus the defect size. The Hill-Sachs lesion is
then measured from the medial edge of the lesion to the rotator cuff insertion (Figure
8). If the Hill-Sachs lesion size is greater than the glenoid track, the shoulder is
considered off track. If the Hill-Sachs lesion size is smaller than the glenoid track, the
shoulder is considered on track. Surgeons must understand how the interaction of
humeral and glenoid bone loss can affect the glenoid track, leading to instability. In
patients with an off-track shoulder, procedures that address glenoid or the humeral
bone loss can be performed to restore stability.

Treatment Options
Arthroscopic or open Bankart repair may be considered in the setting of subcritical
glenoid bone loss without a Hill-Sachs lesion or an on-track shoulder. Recurrence rates
have been reported to be lower than 10% in these patients. In comparing the
arthroscopic technique and open techniques, no differences have been observed in

9/4/26, 10:28 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Instability: Management of Bone Loss and Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000626
16/30

clinical outcomes; however, a reduction in external rotation may be observed after open
repair.8
The surgical plan needs to be individualized to the patient. The Latarjet technique may
be an option in patients with subcritical bone loss, particularly those who are high-level
contact athletes or in whom prior soft-tissue stabilization procedure has failed.6 The
Latarjet technique involves an osteotomy of the coracoid at its base followed by a
transfer of the coracoid and its attached conjoint tendon to the anterior glenoid. This
technique provides stability in several ways. First, the coracoid widens the glenoid track,
which increases the surface area available for the humeral head to articulate. Second,
the conjoint tendon acts as a sling that helps resist anterior translation with the arm
abducted and externally rotated. Lastly, the capsule is repaired at the end of the
procedure, further providing stability.8
For this procedure, the patient is placed in the beach-chair position. Arthroscopy can be
performed initially to evaluate for any intra-articular pathology. After completion of the
arthroscopic portion of the procedure, a deltopectoral approach is performed. The
incision for the Latarjet procedure is extended proximally to gain adequate exposure of
the coracoid (Figure 9).
After dissection to the coracoid has been achieved, the coracoacromial ligament is
identified and cut, leaving a 1-cm cuff that will be secured to the capsule at the end of
the procedure. At this point, the pectoralis minor is released directly from the coracoid.
The soft tissue is released along the inferior surface of the coracoid to feel the base of
the coracoid. Figure 10 shows these soft-tissue attachments to the coracoid.
An osteotomy of the base of the coracoid is performed with the use of a 90° oscillating
saw. Surgeons must ensure the osteotomy is made at the base of the coracoid to
maximize the length of graft, which ideally should be 20 to 30 mm. Figure 11 shows the
coracoid osteotomy.
After the osteotomy has been completed, a Kocher forceps is used to grasp the coracoid
at the base, which is rotated in a manner that allows the inferior surface of the coracoid
to be visualized. Any remaining soft tissue is removed, and a burr can be used to

decorticate the undersurface, which creates a bleeding bone bed. After preparation, a
drill guide can be used to predrill the coracoid graft (Figure 12).
After preparation of the coracoid, attention is shifted to glenoid exposure. The superior
and inferior borders of the subscapularis are exposed. A subscapularis tenotomy or
muscle-splitting approach can be performed to expose the underlying capsule. Figure 13
shows the subscapularis-splitting technique. A capsulotomy is performed and tagged for
later repair.
A burr is used to create a bleeding bone bed along the glenoid defect. The coracoid is
held in the appropriate position with the use of Kirschner wires and secured with the use
of cannulated screws (Figure 14).
After final fixation, the wound is irrigated copiously, and the capsule is closed,
incorporating the remaining coracoacromial ligament. The subscapularis split or
tenotomy is repaired subsequently. The skin is closed, and a dressing is applied. A
shoulder immobilizer is placed.
A shoulder immobilizer typically is used for the first 6 weeks postoperatively. The goals
of early rehabilitation are to protect the subscapularis repair and allow for healing of the
coracoid process. Passive elevation is allowed in the scapular plane, but external rotation
beyond 30° is discouraged. Active and active-assisted ROM exercises are initiated 6
weeks postoperatively and continued until full ROM is achieved. Strengthening is
initiated after full, painless ROM is achieved, typically approximately 3 months
postoperatively. Most patients return to sports 4 to 6 months postoperatively.
Complications are not uncommon with this procedure, and complication rates have
been reported to be as high as 30% in some studies. The most common complications
include axillary and musculocutaneous nerve injuries, recurrent dislocation if the graft is
placed too medial, osteoarthritis if the graft is placed too lateral, and graft resorption.6 In
patients with subcritical bone loss and an off-track shoulder, arthroscopic or open soft-
tissue stabilization can be performed in combination with remplissage to address the
humeral defect. Alternatively, a Latarjet procedure also can be performed.6

In patients with glenoid bone loss of more than 20%, the Latarjet procedure is an
excellent treatment option to address the defect. In patients with severe bone loss
(>30% to 35%) or in patients in whom the Latarjet procedure fails, a distal tibia allograft,
glenoid allograft, or iliac crest bone graft (allograft or autograft) may be an option. The
lateral aspect of the distal tibia serves as a viable osteochondral allograft for the
anteroinferior glenoid. The lateral tibial plafond has a similar radius of curvature to the
glenoid and a cartilaginous surface, making it an excellent option for patients with
severe bone loss. The disadvantages of distal tibia allografts include high cost, potential
lack of biologic incorporation, and risk of disease transmission.6 Figure 15 shows a distal
tibia allograft.
Distal tibia allograft augmentation of the glenoid typically is performed via an open
approach; however, an arthroscopic technique has been described. Wong et al12
reported on the radiographic and clinical outcomes of 73 patients who underwent
arthroscopic stabilization with the use of frozen distal tibia allografts. The patients were
followed for almost 5 years. No recurrent dislocations or nerve injuries were reported,
and the graft union rate was 100% (73 patients). In addition, Western Ontario Shoulder
Instability Index scores and Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire
scores substantially improved postoperatively. Five patients underwent screw removal
because of painful hardware.
Iliac crest autograft also has been used to restore anterior glenoid bone defects.
Variation exists in the technique used for harvesting the graft and the fixation. Open and
arthroscopic fixation have been described with reasonable success in restoring
glenohumeral stability; however, the biggest disadvantage to using iliac crest autograft is
donor site morbidity.4

No difference in clinical outcomes between these procedures
Recurrent instability may occur in as many as 75% of patients with more than 25% bone loss.
Remplissage and the Latarjet procedure are associated with good midterm functional
outcomes for patients with an off-track shoulder with subcritical bone loss.
The Latarjet procedure is associated with excellent functional outcomes at long-term follow-
up, with good return to sport rates.
Distal tibial allograft results in a stable shoulder joint with outcomes similar to those of the
Latarjet procedure.

Outcomes
Remplissage has been compared with the Latarjet procedure in off-track shoulders with
subcritical bone loss. In a comparison study, 189 patients with recurrent instability, off-
track shoulders, and bone loss of less than 25% were reviewed retrospectively. Of the
189 patients, 98 underwent arthroscopic Bankart repair with remplissage and 91
underwent the Latarjet procedure. The patients were followed for a mean of 3 years
postoperatively. No difference in functional outcome scores or recurrence rates was
noted between the two groups; however, the remplissage group had more pain and less
internal rotation in abduction compared with the Latarjet group. A higher complication
rate (12.1%; 11 patients) was observed in the Latarjet group compared with the
remplissage group (1%; 1 patient). The likelihood of recurrence was lower in the Latarjet
group, in patients who had undergone prior instability surgery, patients who were
contact athletes, and patients in whom bone loss was greater than 15%.13
Long-term outcome studies have been conducted on the Latarjet procedure. A recent
systematic review by Hurley et al14 described outcomes and recurrence rates after the
open Latarjet procedure. A total of 845 shoulders were included for analysis, with a
mean follow-up of 16 years. The rate of good or excellent outcomes was 86% (718
patients). The rate of return to sport was 85% (718 patients), and 76% (642 patients)
returned to the same level of play. The recurrent instability rate was 8.5% (71 patients),

A retrospective study compared the open Latarjet procedure with arthroscopic Bankart
repair for anterior shoulder instability. A total of 93 patients who underwent
arthroscopic repair were compared with 93 patients who underwent the Latarjet
procedure. The mean follow-up was 6 years postoperatively. In the arthroscopic group,
22% (20 patients) had recurrent instability, compared with 10% (9 patients) in the
Latarjet group. Independent risk factors for recurrence were contact sports and passive
external rotation greater than 85°. The authors of the study recommend the Latarjet
procedure in patients with an Instability Severity Index Score greater than 3.15
Distal tibia allograft has been compared with the Latarjet procedure for anterior
shoulder instability. A matched cohort analysis of 50 patients who underwent distal tibia
allograft and 50 patients who underwent the Latarjet procedure was conducted. The
patients were followed for a mean of 45 months postoperatively. Patients in both groups
experienced improvements in all outcome measures postoperatively. No difference in
outcome scores or complications was observed between the two groups.16
